Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, revenge-focused ideation about identifiable responsible people is hard to reconcile unless there was clear culpability (e.g. negligence), which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It appears clinically mismatched to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Generalized threat from strangers and scanning faces for danger fit interpersonal assault or public violence better than a child's medical crisis. These threat items imply fear of hostile people in ordinary situations, but the rest of the profile does not provide a coherent bridge from the illness trauma to stranger-based danger expectations.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall could occur, but here it primarily supports the revenge item and interpersonal-threat theme. In combination with the stranger-threat items, it pulls the profile toward an assault/perpetrator formulation rather than a child's illness trauma formulation.

issues.item: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
issues.explanation: Meaning seeking is not inherently maladaptive and, in this profile, sits awkwardly with the otherwise threat-trigger-memory driven formulation; it does not clearly function as an avoidance/safety strategy tied to the selected triggers, threat items, or memory pattern.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance for interpersonal threat in faces/body language is difficult to reconcile with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is more plausibly linked to medical cues, loss cues, or signs of illness rather than hostile people.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Needing to stay alert to fall asleep implies ongoing external danger monitoring; for a trauma centered on a child's illness, this would usually require clearer linkage to caregiving/medical monitoring, which is absent from the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: For the indexed trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, 'anything that reminds me of someone I have lost' implies bereavement/loss rather than ongoing threat or illness trauma. That is a hard-to-explain mismatch unless the child died, which is not the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: Within the overall profile, the dominant theme is fear/hypervigilance/disorientation around threat cues (sirens, crying, startle, sleep vigilance, physical reactivity, confused/unreal memory). 'Intense rage' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile and sits awkwardly beside suppression of anger, making this item clinically less coherent than the others.

vignette: Luis, a 25-year-old data scientist born to Mexican immigrants in a modest apartment on the East Side, left a quiet childhood behind when a sudden heart attack took his 6-year-old brother away. He was only six years old then, and the emergency room's harsh fluorescent lights, the whine of the monitors, and the relentless sirens that punctuated the night were stamped indelibly into his mind. In the years that followed, the memory of that moment became a restless presence, a story that felt unreal, a terror that returned each time he heard the ambulance's wail or felt the faint scent of sweat on a coworker's hand. The first time a siren wafted across the street a year after the loss, Luis felt the familiar jarring startle that had become a hallmark of his anxiety. The sound brought back the disordered sequence of images-his brother's pale face, the doctor's hushed words, the ambulance's flashing lights-and the terror he had felt then. That auditory reminder sparked an immediate urge to suppress the anger he felt toward the doctor and to push the thought of the event out of his mind, for he feared that feeling anger would reopen the wound. This suppression, in turn, kept the memory alive, as the unprocessed fear kept resurfacing. Moreover, the heightened threat vigilance-his constant need to stay alert to any sound-made the siren feel even more dangerous, reinforcing the startle response and the physical reactivity of his muscles. The cycle closed back on the trigger, as the memory's vividness made him even more sensitive to any siren, sweat, or crying, thereby feeding the threat vigilance and prompting him to suppress thoughts and anger. In the same moment, the siren's echo in his mind pushed him to avoid any medical cues, to refuse hospital visits and routine examinations, because each time he faced such cues he would be forced to confront the traumatic scene and his suppressed feelings. Luis's days at the tech firm have become a constant negotiation with these triggers. His office is located in a building that regularly receives ambulances for accidents on the nearby street; the sirens can be heard from his window, causing his heart to leap and his shoulders to tense before he even sits down at his desk. A coworker, Ana, often wears a strong perfume that smells faintly like sweat; when Luis notices the scent, he instinctively steps back, eyes watering, and pulls his laptop aside to avoid the reminder of his brother's illness. He has stopped visiting the company's health clinic for routine check-ups, citing that the waiting room's fluorescent lights and the quiet hum of the machines would make him think of the emergency room. He left an important project incomplete because a sudden cry from the receptionist triggered a panic attack that left him trembling, unable to focus on the data logs. Sleep has become a battle. Luis reports difficulty falling asleep because he needs to stay alert, listening for the siren that could appear at any moment. He wakes up in the night with a racing heart, convinced the world is listening for the ambulance that might come next. The physical reactivity that surfaces-muscle tension, a hot flush when he thinks of the hospital's antiseptic smell-remains a constant companion. All these experiences have woven themselves into his identity as a meticulous, data-driven professional who now feels compelled to suppress anger, thoughts, and any hint of vulnerability in order to keep his mind from slipping back into that night of terror. The weight of these symptoms has finally driven Luis to seek help. For weeks he had been pulling away from his friends, missing deadlines, and becoming increasingly exhausted by the constant need to be vigilant. He has stopped asking for clarifications at work, fearing that the questions would draw attention and trigger his startle response. The realization that he is no longer functioning at the level he once did, that his performance at work is slipping and that his relationship with his family is strained, prompted him to schedule an appointment. Luis most fears that his life will never return to its former calm, and he hopes that by confronting the memory rather than suppressing it, he can finally silence the siren in his mind and feel safe enough to sleep without the dread of an ambulance's wail.
